newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Miners lead Australian stocks to record close.
newsitem.headline: Miners lead Australian stocks to record close.

text.p: The Australian share market locked in a record high closing level on Friday with renewed buying interest in the key resources stocks overcoming a battered banking sector.
The All Ordinaries index added 13.1 to 2538.1, surpassing the previous record closing level of 2,534.3 reached on May 13.
The benchmark index ventured towards the all time high of 2,540.4, also reached on May 13, but stopped just short with an intraday high of 2,539.5

With the big banks bloodied as investors faced up to margin pressures among the financiers, attention turned to the commodity stocks with the growth outlook in the major economies providing the impetus.
"It's the mining stocks that have held it up," said broker Robin Forbes of the Hartley Poynton brokerage, suggesting that recent strength in base metals prices may prove enough to keep the run going.
"There have been good gains in metals prices so maybe that is a foretaste of things to come. If the world economies seem to be improving again then it will lead to increased demand."
The big miners all showed impressive gains.

Bellwether BHP jumped three percent to A$18.689 (US$14.58), CRA climbed nearly two percent to A$20.41, while WMC shot up 2.7 percent to A$8.08. Outside the top rung, base metals and gold miner MIM Holdings added 3.5 percent to A$1.82, while zinc major Pasminco climbed to A$2.72, its highest level since October 1989, before ending five percent higher at A$2.66.
After a sensational run in recent weeks the big banks went the other way with Commonwealth Bank the hardest hit, losing 53 cents or 3.6 percent to close at A$14.12.
ANZ Bank was down 10 cents at A$8.33, while Westpac shed 8.1 to A$7.24. Sector leader National Australia Bank settled below the A$18.00 level, down 16 cents at A$17.95 after going as low as A$17.75.

Insurance group National Mutual Holdings Ltd shares shot to a record high of A$2.10 before ending up four cents at A$1.98 after confirming its 51 percent parent, French-based Axa-UAP, would receive a licence to operate in China.
Rises outnumbered falls by a ratio of about 10 to seven, while 31 percent of stocks traded.
